How to Write a Letter of Intent

A letter of intent is a letter is common in both business and academic contexts. It allows you to demonstrate personality as well as communication skills. A successful letter of intent will be informative, professional, and persuasive.
Here are some steps to follow if you have to write a letter of intent:

1. Make sure you follow all the instructions laid out for you. Visit the business' website for details.
  2. Confirm who you need to address the letter to.
  3. Make notes about what you want to include in your letter. It defines your career objectives and goals, professional experience, leadership skills, and unique attributes to set you apart from the rest.
  4. Personalize the letter.
  5. Be specific about why you are writing the letter, your credentials and why you want to focus on that particular company.
  6. Request a response from the company in your conclusion.
Modals and Other Verbs for Ability, Quality and Achievement
You use modals to talk about ability, natural or learned. You can talk about quantity and achievement in other ways.
The modals can and could and be able to express ability, in the present, past and future.

For example:
When I was a child I could play piano very well.
I can envision myself working at your company for a long time.
I will be able to exceed your expectations and contribute to the success of your company.

Note:
be able to is a very flexible modal - it can be used to talk about the past, present and future.
For Example:
Present: I am not able to sing very well.
Past: When I was five, I was able to play a sonata.
Future: After my leg heals, I will be able to run again.

You can use other verbs such as managed to, succeed in to talk about achievement.

For example:

When I was at the company, I managed to reach all sales goals.
He succeeded in making the company what it is today.

Kristi Lenard
234 Wellington Blvd.
Boston, Massachusetts
E-mail Address: kristi@teleworm.com

Feb 3rd, 2012

Recruitment Officer
Pamela Marshall
BFP Publishing
352 Front St.
Boston, Massachusetts 10011

Sub: Application for the position of Junior Editor

Dear Ms. Marshall,

I write this e-mail in response to an internal advertisement for the post of Junior Editor at BFP publishing. A Harvard English program graduate, with prior experience working in BFP's editing department, I believe that the skills and expertise gained make me an ideal candidate for the post.

On completion of my English degree, I proceeded to complete a number of postgraduate courses in literature, creative writing and publishing. In addition, I commenced an internship at Polygon which honed my skills in a fast-paced environment. Furthermore, the internship enhanced my interpersonal abilities and brought out my flare for efficient and engaging writing and attention to detail.

My time at BFP Publishing has further refined my skills in the publishing field. In fact, I was recently recognized for my valuable contribution to Richard Duncan's new novel and have succeeded in establishing myself as a valuable member of the editing team. I can envision myself working at BFP long term and feel that a Junior Editor position could be a chance to not only demonstrate my commitment to the company but also show my diverse range of communication skills.

As the position commences next month, I will have finished all of my current projects and responsibilities and will have also completed a short course in advanced proofreading skills. I am confident that with my talents, experience and qualifications, I will be able to exceed your expectations and contribute towards greater success of the department. I would therefore like to request an opportunity to discuss the suitability of my candidature. I have enclosed my resume and references for your perusal and will be eagerly awaiting your response.

Thanking you for taking the time to consider my application and I'll be looking forward to speaking with you after the application deadline.

Yours sincerely,

Kristi Lenard
